card.official_title: PROVIDES PERMANENT FUNDING FOR SCHOOLS AND HEALTH CARE BY EXTENDING EXISTING TAX ON HIGH INCOMES. INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
card.plain_title: Make existing higher income tax rates permanent
card.yes_means: The existing higher income tax rates on high-income taxpayers would become permanent instead of expiring in 2031.
card.no_means: The higher income tax rates would remain temporary and expire in 2031 under current law.

what_changes.today: Higher rates paid by the top 2 percent of taxpayers are scheduled to expire in 2031.
what_changes.if_passes: Those existing higher rates would continue permanently.
what_changes.label: fact

what_changes.today: Revenue from the temporary higher rates is scheduled to end when they expire.
what_changes.if_passes: The state would retain an estimated $5 billion to $15 billion each year after the scheduled expiration.
what_changes.label: prediction

what_changes.today: The Constitution sets a minimum funding level for schools and community colleges.
what_changes.if_passes: Roughly 40 percent of the retained revenue would go to schools and community colleges.
what_changes.label: prediction

what_changes.today: Income taxes support health care and other services through the state's main operating account.
what_changes.if_passes: The remaining revenue would support other state programs, with part set aside in budget reserves.
what_changes.label: prediction

who_is_affected: High-income taxpayers who pay the temporary higher rates
Public school and community college students and staff
People who rely on Medi-Cal and other state services

fiscal_impact.text: Making the rates permanent would preserve an estimated $5 billion to $15 billion in annual state income tax revenue after their scheduled expiration; the amount would vary widely by year.
fiscal_impact.label: prediction

steelman_yes.headline: Supporters argue it would protect school funding and help prevent teacher layoffs, crowded classrooms, and cuts to student services.
more_reasons: Supporters argue it keeps existing rates on the top 2 percent of taxpayers rather than raising current rates.
Supporters emphasize local control of school funds, audits, and limits on administrative spending as safeguards for classroom funding.

best_evidence.text: The measure would preserve $5 billion to $15 billion a year, with roughly 40 percent supporting schools and community colleges.
best_evidence.label: prediction

best_evidence.text: The higher rates apply to the top 2 percent of California taxpayers.
best_evidence.label: fact

steelman_yes.who_it_helps: Supporters say students, families relying on health care, and communities using public services would benefit.
steelman_yes.answer_to_other_side: Supporters argue that keeping current rates avoids a future tax cut for high-income taxpayers that would put classroom and health care funding at risk.

steelman_no.headline: Opponents argue it would keep higher rates voters were told were temporary, instead of allowing scheduled tax relief.
more_reasons: Opponents argue that keeping higher taxes makes California more expensive for affected taxpayers.
Opponents argue that spending controls and better results from existing funding should come before a permanent revenue commitment.

best_evidence.text: The measure replaces the scheduled 2031 expiration with permanent higher income tax rates.
best_evidence.label: fact

best_evidence.text: Opponents say the state should get spending under control before voters approve permanently higher taxes.
best_evidence.label: value
best_evidence.whose: Opponents in the official ballot argument

steelman_no.who_it_helps: Opponents say rejection would help affected taxpayers by preserving the scheduled end of higher rates.
steelman_no.answer_to_other_side: Opponents argue that better spending controls should protect services, rather than permanently extending taxes to sustain current spending.

crux.text: The sides disagree about whether preserving public-service revenue is worth giving up the scheduled tax reduction. They also disagree about whether losing that revenue would require service cuts or could be managed through better spending controls.

evidence.text: The measure keeps existing higher rates; it does not increase them now, but it prevents their scheduled expiration in 2031.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.text: The taxpayers who pay these higher rates account for about half of all state income taxes.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.text: Revenue would vary widely because much of the taxed income is tied to the stock market; permanent rates would not guarantee a steady annual amount.
evidence.label: prediction

evidence.text: Roughly 40 percent of the retained revenue would support schools and community colleges; the rest would support other programs and budget reserves.
evidence.label: prediction

turing_yes.reason: It captures the main merits case in the official Yes argument: keeping the existing rates would preserve revenue for schools and health care without raising rates now, and it includes the supporters’ accountability and local-control points. It could be more careful to keep the service-cut claims clearly attributed to supporters, as it generally does.

turing_no.reason: It fairly includes tax relief and spending discipline, but omits a central No argument in the official argument: voters were told the higher rates were temporary, so making them permanent breaks that commitment. The headline instead frames the case only as denying taxpayers a scheduled tax reduction.

swap_notes: The Yes headline leads with protecting schools and preventing cuts, while the No headline uses the more adversarial phrase “permanently deny affected taxpayers the tax reduction.” Both positions are attributed, but the No headline does not present the No side’s central temporary-commitment argument. Revise for comparable, merits-focused framing.
loaded_or_overconfident: “Permanently deny” is a loaded framing of the scheduled tax reduction. Consider neutral wording such as “would keep the higher rates in place after 2031.”
verdict.instructions: 1. Revise the No headline to include the No side’s central argument that voters were told the higher rates would be temporary, alongside its case for tax relief or spending controls; keep it parallel in tone to the Yes headline. 2. Replace “permanently deny” with neutral wording, such as “keep the higher rates in place after 2031.”

turing_yes.reason: Fairly presents the supporters’ central merits case: keeping the existing rates preserves revenue for schools and other services, and supporters say that can help avert school cuts. It also includes the existing-rate and accountability arguments. It could more clearly include supporters’ health-care case, but the card does mention health-care beneficiaries.

turing_no.reason: Fairly presents the opponents’ core trade-off: the rates were temporary, keeping them means forgoing the scheduled expiration, and spending controls should come before a permanent revenue commitment. It also notes the cost-of-living concern. This is a solid summary of the official opposition arguments.
